text: After Teginabad's flat customs-wall discipline - and the particular tired patience of the amid who'd measured him there, Sa'id ibn Yaqub, closing his ledger over a question he'd chosen not to press further - Bost announced Ghaznavid wealth a different way - not with a gate and a ledger, but with a skyline. Across the canal-fed green, low domes and a long red-brick palace face caught the last sun: the sultan's winter residence, Lashkari Bazar, more garrison-town than palace grounds, more market than either. Farrukh had no business inside those walls and no wish to acquire any. His business was smaller, and stranger: a piece of paper from a house in Rayy that his father's accounts should never have mentioned.

His business was smaller, and stranger: a piece of paper from a house in Rayy that his father's accounts should never have mentioned. He was still turning the Rayy paper over in his mind, standing in front of all that brick to do it, when he noticed he had started counting instead, and was some way in before he understood what he was counting. Eleven men on foot, somewhere back along the desert road, whom he had numbered aloud for the keeper of a watchpost on the last stretch because the man had asked him and was entitled to ask and had nothing whatever to write the answer down on. The keeper's own pay had not reached his post since before the summer, by his own flat account of it, and he had asked after the road behind the caravan the way a man asks after anything that might turn out to be news. Farrukh had answered him fully and thought nothing much of it at the time. Watching the last of the sun go along a palace face laid up in courses that had plainly not waited on anybody's pay, he found he was thinking something of it now.

text: Every winter-quartered army needs men who can turn one kingdom's coin into another's, and Bost had no shortage of them. Farrukh found the one the caravan drivers trusted on reputation alone - a narrow shopfront off the bazaar's spine, scales hung by the door, a small clay lamp burning steadily beside the account-books that Farrukh noticed but did not ask about, and a {{sarraf|sarraf}} named Mihran who weighed silver for a living and, by the look of the room, had done it long enough to stop being impressed by anyone's coin.

text: Before Farrukh could say why he'd come, Mihran glanced at the pouch on his belt - the same unspoken question, Farrukh guessed, that any sarraf put to a travel-worn stranger before business of any other kind. "Thorough, or quick?" Mihran asked, already reaching for his scale. "Thorough, I check every coin against the stones myself. Costs a little more. Quick, I go by eye - and my eye is usually right, for what that's worth to you."

text: Mihran's hands stopped on one coin before it reached the rest. He turned it once in the lamp-light, weighed it apart from the others, and set it down instead of adding it to the stack. "Someone's had a knife at the edge of this," he said, not looking up - clipped, the silver shaved thin enough to matter, however carefully the theft had been dressed up as ordinary wear. His thumb found the stamp next. "And I haven't taken coin from this mint in two years - not since the man whose name is on it stopped being anyone's idea of an authority worth trusting. Whoever's name gets struck into new coin is making a promise, same as any paper. Some promises age worse than others."

text: "Two amirs, both claiming the same stretch of road, each striking coin with his own name on it," Mihran said, setting the light coin aside for melting rather than spending. "Merchants don't wait for anyone to settle that properly. We decide for ourselves whose promise to trust with our own scales. It settles itself, eventually - one name stops appearing on new coin, and everyone quietly agrees to remember why." He shrugged, already reaching for the next coin in the stack. "Nothing personal in it, when I don't take his either."

text: He worked as he talked, unbothered by silence but not opposed to filling it either. "Where are you bound?" Farrukh said Farah, and past it, though not why. Mihran nodded like he'd heard the shape of that answer before. "Then you're carrying your coin the wrong way," he said. "Every dirham on you past here is a dirham a bad road or a worse man can take from you. Men who move money seriously don't carry it at all - they carry paper. A letter naming a sum, and a name in some other city who already owes the man who wrote it that much, or trusts him enough to advance it without asking why. The coin never travels. Only the promise does, city to city, banker to banker, on nothing but each man's word that the last one was good for it." He said it the way a man recites something true and faintly boring - a fact of his trade, not a marvel. Farrukh set his father's suftaja on the counter without a word. The same kind of paper Mihran had just finished describing. He suspected this one would not turn out to be boring at all.

text: He set the paper down without being asked and looked at Farrukh properly for the first time. "Ibn Hasan," he said - not a question. "You have his hands. He came through here four, five years running, always the same honest weight, never once tried to pass me clipped silver like half these road-merchants do. I am sorry for him. Whatever this is" - he touched the paper again, carefully, as if it might be warm - "he did not deserve to carry it alone. Whether he understood he was carrying it at all, I couldn't say."

text: Mihran set the last of Farrukh's coin aside and, in the same unhurried voice he'd used for everything else that afternoon, mentioned he had a merchant contact bound for Herat who could use a second pair of hands he trusted - someone to mind a share of the goods the rest of the way, for a cut of whatever they sold for. "{{mudaraba|Mudaraba}}," he said, when Farrukh asked what to call it. "His capital, your carrying. If it turns a profit, you take a share of it. If it doesn't - and roads like this one don't always let it - the loss is his to carry, not yours, provided you haven't been careless with what he trusted you to carry. That's the whole of the arrangement. Older than either of our fathers, and it still works exactly that plainly."

text: Farrukh left Mihran's shop as the winter light went copper over Lashkari Bazar's long brick face, close enough now to make out painted guardsmen on the palace's outer wall - a hundred still figures keeping a watch that had never once been real. He thought of what it must have cost, all of it - the paint, the brick, the canals, the garrison that ate a season's wages just by existing - and did not let himself finish the thought all the way to where it wanted to go. That accounting was for another day, on another road. Tonight there was only Farah ahead, and a channel somewhere with his father's name written on it in water.

text: A familiar face crossed his path near the bazaar's edge - the same agent from Teginabad's stall, Yusuf, visibly as surprised as Farrukh was to find the road had crossed itself again so soon. Neither had seen the other since that stall, and each had crossed the desert stretch between with nothing but his own guide and his own caravan for company - which made meeting again feel less like coincidence and more like the road simply insisting on itself. They traded a few words, an uncle's business Yusuf still didn't elaborate on, and a shared understanding, unspoken, that neither expected this to be the last time.

text: He found the yard where his new guide was loading the last of the mules for a dawn start already sharing space with a scatter of Nasa herders camped along its far wall, watching their own animals with the flat, unhurried patience of people who had done this every night of their working lives and expected to keep doing it for exactly as long as the alternative stayed worse. His guide, following his glance, said only what everyone stopping here already seemed to know: the family's usual grazing had run along a border the last two seasons' fighting had redrawn without asking anyone who actually lived on it, and the road west - the same road Farrukh meant to take at first light - was not nearly as empty, these days, as it used to be.

text: His new guide was a Farah man who wanted to be in Farah, and he set a pace that left Farrukh most of the first morning with nothing to do but look at the ground, which was how he came to spend the better part of it thinking about dung. There was a great deal of it, and it was not lying where a caravan leaves it. It ran in a broken line along the north verge and out into the scrub beyond, and when he turned the heaps over with a stick the older ones were dry the whole way through and the newer ones were not, and one of them, past the second windbreak, still held a little heat under the shell of it. Small pellets ran among the large ones the entire way along. A patch of thin winter grazing beside the track had been cropped to the root and then past the root, the roots themselves pulled and the ground left looking scalped. A hobble-rope was knotted around a tamarisk stump and left knotted, which is not what a man does to a rope he means to use again. And in the windbreak's shade a goat's kid stood by itself with its head down, too young to have come far and too young to be worth anybody going back for, and did not move at all as the mules went by.

choices.text: A drover took a flock down to the army's market, and made poor work of it.

text: He came up on them at the second channel-head, where a line of tamarisk had been put in by somebody's grandfather to keep the sand off the water, and they did not gather the flock in when they saw the caravan, which told him something about how many caravans had already gone past them. An old woman did the talking. Behind her were two grown sons, a daughter-in-law, four children of assorted heights, one camel under a pack-saddle it had clearly been wearing for days, and perhaps thirty head of sheep and goats standing about in the patient, stupid way of animals walked further than they would choose. Nasa people, by the accent. Their winter grazing along the lower channels had been set aside for the wintering army's remounts and baggage animals - lawfully, with the order read out in the village and a share of the flock taken against a tally and a remission promised on next year's assessment, all of which she recited to him in the level voice of a woman who had stopped expecting the recitation to move anybody. They were walking to her daughter-in-law's cousin, three days on. They had nothing to sell him and nothing to threaten him with, and he understood, listening to her, that if she asked him for anything at all it would be water for the children and not a mouthful for the flock, because a stranger who is asked for animals hears a man asking him for money.

text: What she asked for, once she had thanked him and got past thanking him, was an hour of his guide's time, and she asked it badly, the way people ask who are not used to asking strangers for anything that cannot simply be handed over. The good water on this stretch had stopped being merely the good water. Two of the cisterns had been taken up by the remount lines at the hours when animals actually want to drink; a third had gone brackish in a way she had heard about at the last village and had no means of confirming; and the channel-heads ran or did not run according to arrangements made in Bost by men who had never seen them. His guide knew all of it, in the way of a man who had walked the road forty times, and it was precisely and entirely what Farrukh was paying him for - he had bought this man's knowledge of the water, and the man was already making it plain, without troubling to say a word, that he did not regard it as Farrukh's to give away. It would cost an hour of daylight and the goodwill of somebody he had three more days of. It would cost nothing that could be written down anywhere at all, and Farrukh noticed that he was working out the price of it regardless, out of habit, like a man counting change he has already been given.

text: The relay post stood where the tracks crossed a dry channel a half-day short of Farah - mud brick, one room, a well with a wooden lid, and a road-warden who came out with his charcoal already in his hand. He wanted the caravan's origin, its owner's name, the number of men, the number of beasts, and what stock had come up the road behind it. He kept his count on the whitewashed plaster inside his own doorway, in columns, because paper had to be asked for from Bost and asking for it made a man memorable to people he would rather stayed vague about him. He explained this to Farrukh at some length while writing, being lonely, and explained further that the numbers went up at the turn of the year and settled what fodder this stretch of road would be assessed for and what the post might keep back for itself, so that a warden who wrote down too little starved his own well in the summer, and one who wrote down too much was a liar for the remainder of his working life. The last of the questions he put in exactly the same voice as the others, which was the whole difficulty with it. Nobody was going to be arrested over a column on a wall. Farrukh had the number in his head, and had had it since the first morning.
